questionText: A two-digit number ♣9 is multiplied by a three-digit number ♣♣3. The digits in the ♣ place are not necessarily the same. Which of the following can be the product of the given two numbers?
hints: Check the LAST digit first (9 × 3). Then check the smallest and largest possible products to rule out options that are too small or too big.
Smallest product = 19 × 103 = 1957. Largest product = 99 × 993 = 98,307.

stepByStep.text: Last digit: 9 × 3 = 27 → ends in 7 (all options end in 7, so size must decide).
1907 and 957 are smaller than the smallest possible product 1957 ✗.
756927 is bigger than the largest possible product (about 98,300) ✗.
Only 46847 is left ✓ (it equals 79 × 593).

questionText: How many weeks are there in 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 minutes?
hints: Work out how many minutes there are in ONE week (7 days × 24 hours × 60 minutes). Then divide.
1 week = 7 × 24 × 60 = 10080 minutes.

stepByStep.text: 1 week = 7 × 24 × 60 = 10080 minutes.

questionText: A three-digit number ♣♣7 is multiplied by a two-digit number ♣8. The digits in ♣ place are not necessarily the same. Which of the following can be the product of the given two numbers?
hints: Check the last digit (7 × 8). Then check the smallest and the biggest possible product to throw out the rest.
Smallest product = 107 × 18 = 1926. Largest product = 997 × 98 = 97,706.

stepByStep.text: Last digit: 7 × 8 = 56 → ends in 6. That removes 29405 (ends in 5).
1906 is smaller than the smallest possible product (1926) ✗.
977706 is bigger than the largest possible product (97,706) ✗.
Only 52606 is left ✓ (it equals 58 × 907).

questionText: In a basket 104 mangoes are there. If you take out 4 mangoes and replace them by 3 apples, till all mangoes are removed out of the basket, then how many apples will be there in the basket at the end?
hints: How many times can you take out 4 mangoes from 104? Each time puts in 3 apples.
Number of swaps = 104 ÷ 4. Apples = swaps × 3.

stepByStep.text: Apples = 26 × 3 = 78.

questionText: A hospital stores one type of medicine in a 2-decagram container. How many 1-milligram doses are there in a 2-decagram container?
hints: 1 decagram = 10 grams. And 1 gram = 1000 milligrams. Change decagrams to grams, then to milligrams.
1 decagram = 10 g = 10,000 mg.

stepByStep.text: 2 decagram = 2 × 10 = 20 grams.
20 grams = 20 × 1000 = 20,000 milligrams.
Number of 1 mg doses = 20000.

questionText: When a number X is divided by 5 the remainder is 2. When another number Y is divided by 5 the remainder is 4. When you divide X + Y by 5, then what should be the remainder?
hints: Pick real numbers: X = 7 (remainder 2) and Y = 9 (remainder 4). Add them and divide by 5.
Remainders can be added, then divided by 5 again.

stepByStep.text: Try real numbers. 7 leaves remainder 2 when divided by 5, and 9 leaves remainder 4. So take X as 7 and Y as 9.
Then X + Y is 7 + 9 = 16.
16 is 3 fives (15) and 1 more, so the remainder is 1.
It works for any such numbers: the remainders add to 2 + 4 = 6, and 6 is one five and 1 more. So the remainder is 1.

questionText: What least number should be subtracted from 13601, so that the remainder is divisible by 87?
hints: Divide 13601 by 87. The remainder is exactly the number you need to subtract.
Number − remainder is a multiple of the divisor.

stepByStep.text: Divide 13601 by 87. The remainder is what must be taken away.
87 × 156 = 13572. That is the largest multiple of 87 that fits into 13601, because the next one, 87 × 157 = 13659, is too big.
13601 − 13572 = 29, so the remainder is 29.
So 29 must be subtracted.

questionText: A two-digit number (♣8) is multiplied by a three-digit number (♣♣6). Which of the following can be their product if ♣ represents a digit, not necessarily the same?
hints: Check the last digit (8 × 6). Then check the smallest and biggest possible products to rule out the rest.
Smallest product = 18 × 106 = 1908. Largest product = 98 × 996 = 97,608.

stepByStep.text: Last digit: 8 × 6 = 48 → ends in 8. That removes 79764 (ends in 4).
1808 is smaller than the smallest possible product (1908) ✗.
970608 is bigger than the largest possible product (97,608) ✗.
Only 50808 is left ✓ (it equals 58 × 876).

hints: Work out the top (multiply) and the bottom (add) separately. The bottom is 1 + 2 + … + 8; use pairs to add quickly.
Sum of 1 to n = n × (n + 1) ÷ 2.

questionText: When 2000 is divided by a certain number, the quotient is 29 and the remainder is 57. Find the square of the divisor.
hints: Use the division rule: Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder. Put in 2000, 29 and 57 and find the divisor.
Dividend = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder.

questionText: What will be the remainder when the product of all one-digit odd numbers is divided by 18?
hints: One-digit odd numbers: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. Multiply them all, then divide by 18 and see what is left over.
Remainder = Dividend − (Divisor × whole-number quotient).

stepByStep.text: Remainder = 945 − 936 = 9.

questionText: A three-digit number (**7) is multiplied by a three-digit number (**6). Which of the following can be their product if * represents a digit, not necessarily the same?
hints: Check the last digit (7 × 6), then check the smallest possible product (107 × 106) and the largest (997 × 996).
Smallest product = 107 × 106 = 11342. Largest product = 997 × 996 = 993,012.

stepByStep.text: Ones digit: 7 × 6 = 42 → product ends in 2. That removes 457647 (ends in 7).
Smallest possible = 107 × 106 = 11342, so 11332 is too small ✗.
Largest possible = 997 × 996 = 993012, so 994312 is too big ✗.
Only 353362 is left ✓ (it equals 547 × 646).

questionText: How many fifteens make up twelve hundreds?
hints: Twelve hundreds is a number: 12 × 100. The question asks how many 15s fit into it, so this is a division.
Write twelve hundreds as 1200. Now divide 1200 by 15. It can help to think of 1200 as 120 tens.
A similar one: how many fives make six hundreds? 600 ÷ 5 = 120, and 120 is 12 tens.

stepByStep.text: Twelve hundreds = 12 × 100 = 1200.
Count the fifteens in 1200: 1200 ÷ 15 = 80.
80 is the same as 8 tens. So 8 tens of fifteens make up twelve hundreds.

misconceptions.A: 8 is the digit but without the unit. 1200÷15 = 80 = 8 Tens.
misconceptions.C: This is the correct answer. 8T = 8 Tens = 80, and 15 × 80 = 1200.

questionText:
Multiply the two numbers by inserting proper digits in place of the asterisks and find the product.
  5 ✻ 7
×   4 ✻
------
✻ 5 8 ✻
+ ✻ ✻ 0 ✻ 0
---------
2 2 ✻ 6 1
hints: Start from the units. The last digit of the product is 1, and it comes from 7 times the units digit of the second number. Which digit times 7 ends in 1?
7 × 3 = 21, so the second number is 43. The first row is 5✻7 × 3 and it must look like ✻58✻. Try the missing digit until the row fits, then multiply by 43.
Example: in 3✻ × 3 = 1✻1, the product ends in 1, so the star times 3 must end in 1. Only 7 × 3 = 21 does that. Check: 37 × 3 = 111, which fits the pattern.

stepByStep.text: Units digit of product is 1. 7×?=?1. Only 7×3=21 works. Multiplier units=3.
Multiplier = 43. From partial product row 1 (*58*): 5_7 × 3 = _58_. Try 527×3=1581 ✓

misconceptions.D: The answer is 22661, which IS option A.

questionText: A factory makes 1720 boxes every day. What is the total production in the month of July?
hints: July has 31 days. Total = 1720 × 31.
Break it down: 1720 × 30 + 1720 × 1
Try: 100 boxes/day × 31 days = 3100 boxes.

stepByStep.text: July has 31 days

questionText: The product of two numbers is 108. If one of the numbers is doubled and the other is tripled, what will the new product be?
hints: You do not need to know the two numbers. Think about what happens to a product when one of its numbers is made 2 times as big, and the other 3 times as big.
Doubling one number doubles the product. Tripling the other number then triples it again. So the new product is 2 × 3 = 6 times the old product of 108.
Example: 4 × 5 = 20. Double the 4 and triple the 5: 8 × 15 = 120. That is 6 times 20, because 2 × 3 = 6.

stepByStep.text: Doubling one number makes the product 2 times as big. Tripling the other makes it 3 times as big again.
So the new product is 2 × 3 = 6 times the old product.
6 × 108 = 648. So the new product is 648.

misconceptions.D: This is the correct answer. Doubling one and tripling the other multiplies the product by 6.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (product digit analysis)
questionText: Which of the following could be the product of ✻✻6 and ✻9 if the asterisk denotes digits not necessarily the same?
hints: Look at the last digits first. The product of a number ending in 6 and a number ending in 9 must end in the same digit as 6 × 9.
6 × 9 = 54, so the product ends in 4. That leaves two of the choices. Now think about size: can a three-digit number times a two-digit number have six digits?
Example: could ✻3 × ✻4 be 345? 3 × 4 = 12, so the product must end in 2. 345 ends in 5, so it is not a match.

stepByStep.text: Last digits: 6 × 9 = 54, so the product must end in 4. This rules out 5417 and 86996.
Size: the biggest possible product is 996 × 99 = 98604, which has five digits. So the six-digit number 357604 is too big.
Check the one that is left: 176 × 29 = 5104, and 176 and 29 fit the patterns. So the product could be 5104.

misconceptions.A: 5417 ends in 7, but 6×9=54, product must end in 4.
misconceptions.B: This is the correct answer. 176×29=5104, matching ✻✻6 × ✻9.
misconceptions.C: 86996 ends in 6, not 4, and exceeds max possible product.
misconceptions.D: 357604 is too large for a 3-digit × 2-digit multiplication.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (product digit analysis)
questionText: What can be the possible product of ✻✻7 × ✻4 from the given alternatives when ✻ denotes digits not necessarily the same?
hints: Look at the last digits first. The product of a number ending in 7 and a number ending in 4 must end in the same digit as 7 × 4.
7 × 4 = 28, so the product ends in 8. Three choices still fit. Now think about size: what are the smallest and the biggest products a three-digit number times a two-digit number can give?
Example: could ✻✻2 × ✻3 be 986? It ends in 6 and 2 × 3 = 6, so the ending fits. But the smallest such product is 102 × 13 = 1326, so 986 is too small.

stepByStep.text: Last digits: 7 × 4 = 28, so the product must end in 8. This rules out 35271.
Smallest possible product: 107 × 14 = 1498, so 1398 is too small. Biggest possible: 997 × 94 = 93718, so 104978 is too big.
Check the one that is left: 257 × 64 = 16448, and 257 and 64 fit the patterns. So the product can be 16448.

misconceptions.A: 104978 exceeds the maximum possible product of a 3-digit × 2-digit number.
misconceptions.B: 35271 ends in 1, but 7×4=28, so product must end in 8.

questionText: In a bundle of notes of Rs. 5 denomination, the notes are numbered serially from 40801 to 40901. What is the total amount of money in this bundle?
hints: How many notes are there from 40801 to 40901?
Try: notes from 1 to 5 = 5 notes. 5×Rs.5 = Rs.25.

stepByStep.text: Count the notes from 40801 to 40901. Subtract and add 1, because both the first and the last note are counted: 40901 − 40801 + 1 = 101 notes.
Each note is worth Rs. 5, so multiply: 101 × 5 = 505.
So the bundle holds Rs. 505 in all.

misconceptions.A: Rs.500 = 100×5, off by one (forgetting the +1 in counting).
misconceptions.B: This is the correct answer. 101 notes × Rs.5 = Rs.505.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (division with remainder)
questionText: When 18 girls are made to stand in each row, 30 rows can be formed. If 26 girls are made to stand in each row, 21 rows are formed but the 21st row falls short of some number of girls. How many more girls are needed to complete that row?
hints: The number of girls does not change. First find how many girls there are from the 18-in-a-row arrangement.
There are 18 × 30 = 540 girls. With 26 in a row, 20 full rows use 26 × 20 = 520 girls. How many girls are left for the 21st row, and how many short of 26 is that?
Example: 12 children stand 5 in a row. Two full rows use 10 children, so the 3rd row has 2. It needs 5 − 2 = 3 more children to be complete.

stepByStep.text: 540 ÷ 26 = 20 remainder 20
Girls needed = 26 − 20 = 6

misconceptions.B: 20 is the remainder, not how many more are needed.
misconceptions.C: This is the correct answer. 26−20=6 more girls needed.
misconceptions.D: 9 might come from a calculation error.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (division with remainder)
questionText: A 10 metre long wire is cut into 7 equal parts, each a whole number of centimetres long. What is the minimum length of the wire that would be left over?
hints: Change the wire's length to centimetres first. To leave as little wire as possible, the 7 equal parts must be as long as they can be.
10 metres is 1000 cm. Divide 1000 by 7. The whole-number part tells you how long each piece is, and the remainder is the wire left over.
A similar one: a 50 cm ribbon is cut into 6 equal pieces, each a whole number of centimetres. 6 × 8 = 48, so each piece is 8 cm and 50 − 48 = 2 cm is left over.

stepByStep.text: Change metres to centimetres: 10 m is 1000 cm.
The 7 parts should be as long as possible. 7 × 142 = 994, and 7 × 143 = 1001 is more than 1000, so each part is 142 cm.
Wire left over: 1000 − 994 = 6. So the minimum length left over is 6 cm.

misconceptions.A: 3 cm would mean 1000−3=997 is divisible by 7, but 997÷7=142.4.
misconceptions.B: This is the correct answer. 1000 mod 7 = 6.

questionText: When a number is divided by 11, the quotient is equal to the divisor and the remainder is 2 less than the divisor. Find that number.
hints: Divisor = 11, Quotient = 11 (equal to divisor), Remainder = 11−2 = 9.
Number = Divisor × Quotient + Remainder = 11 × 11 + 9.
Try: divided by 5, quotient=5, remainder=3. Number = 5×5+3=28.

stepByStep.text: Quotient = Divisor = 11
Remainder = 11 − 2 = 9

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (finding the divisor)
questionText: When 3000 is divided by a certain number, the quotient obtained is 76 and the remainder is 36. Find the divisor.
hints: In any division: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder. Here you know the dividend, the quotient and the remainder.
Take the remainder away first: 3000 − 36 = 2964. This is exactly divisor × 76. So divide 2964 by 76.
Example: 50 divided by a number gives quotient 6 and remainder 2. 50 − 2 = 48, and 48 ÷ 6 = 8, so the divisor is 8. Check: 8 × 6 + 2 = 50.

misconceptions.B: 36 is the remainder, not the divisor.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (division error correction)
questionText: While carrying out division, a student took 24 instead of 42 as the divisor. His quotient was 91. What was the correct answer had he not committed the mistake?
hints: The student divided some number by 24 and got 91. What number was he dividing?
Try: wrong divisor 3 gives Q=10 → number=30. Correct divisor 6: 30÷6=5.

stepByStep.text: Find the number being divided. The student divided it by 24 and got 91, so the number is 24 × 91 = 2184.
Now divide by the correct divisor: 2184 ÷ 42 = 52.
So the correct answer was 52.

misconceptions.B: 19 might come from a different calculation error.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (operation error correction)
questionText: Instead of multiplying, a student divided a number by 13 and got 11 as the quotient and 4 as the remainder. What was the correct answer to the problem?
hints: First find the number the student started with. In a division: number = divisor × quotient + remainder.
The number is 13 × 11 + 4. Work that out. Then do what the student was meant to do: multiply that number by 13.
Example: a student divided a number by 5 and got quotient 3 and remainder 1. The number is 5 × 3 + 1 = 16. He should have multiplied: 16 × 5 = 80.

stepByStep.text: Find the number: divisor × quotient + remainder = 13 × 11 + 4 = 143 + 4 = 147.
The student should have multiplied this number by 13: 147 × 13 = 1911.
So the correct answer to the problem was 1911.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (division error correction)
questionText: Instead of dividing a number by 12, a student divided it by 18 and got 71 as the quotient and 6 as the remainder. Had he divided the original number by 12, what would the remainder be?
hints: First find the number the student was dividing. In a division: number = divisor × quotient + remainder.
The number is 18 × 71 + 6. Work that out, then divide it by 12 and see what is left over.
Example: a number divided by 7 gives quotient 4 and remainder 2, so it is 7 × 4 + 2 = 30. Divide 30 by 4 instead: 4 × 7 = 28, and 30 − 28 = 2 is left over.

stepByStep.text: 1284 ÷ 12 = 107 remainder 0
Remainder = 0

misconceptions.A: 6 is the remainder from the wrong division, not the correct one.
misconceptions.D: This is the correct answer. 1284÷12=107 exactly.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (finding missing factor)
questionText: The continuous product of three numbers is 2880. If two of the numbers are 12 and 15, find the third.
hints: Three numbers multiplied together give 2880. If you know two of them, dividing the product by those two leaves the third.
Multiply the two known numbers: 12 × 15 = 180. Now work out how many 180s make 2880.
Example: the product of three numbers is 60 and two of them are 3 and 4. 3 × 4 = 12, and 60 ÷ 12 = 5, so the third number is 5.

misconceptions.D: 16 IS option B, so 'none' is wrong.

questionText: In Grade 5, there are 72 students. If each student has to be given 7 chocolates, how many dozens of chocolates will you require?
hints: First find the total number of chocolates needed. Then change that total into dozens. One dozen is 12.
72 students each get 7 chocolates, so you need 72 × 7 chocolates. Then divide that total by 12 to get dozens.
Example: 24 children each get 3 sweets. That is 24 × 3 = 72 sweets, and 72 ÷ 12 = 6, so you need 6 dozen.

misconceptions.D: This is the correct answer. 504÷12=42 dozens.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (difference of products)
questionText: When a number is multiplied by 35 instead of 53, the product obtained is less than the original product by 378. What is the number?
hints: Multiplying by 53 gives 53 lots of the number. Multiplying by 35 gives only 35 lots. How many lots of the number went missing?
53 − 35 = 18, so the product is short by 18 lots of the number. Those 18 lots add up to 378. Divide to find one lot.
Example: a number multiplied by 4 instead of 7 gives a product that is 30 less. 7 − 4 = 3 lots are missing, so the number is 30 ÷ 3 = 10.

stepByStep.text: Multiplying by 35 instead of 53 leaves out 53 − 35 = 18 lots of the number.
Those 18 lots make up the difference of 378, so the number is 378 ÷ 18 = 21.

misconceptions.B: 18 is the difference of multipliers, not the number.

subTopic: Grade 5 — Multiplication and division (replacement word problem)
questionText: In a basket, there are 56 apples. Amey takes out 4 apples at a time and replaces them with 3 oranges. He continues this process till all the apples in the basket are replaced. How many oranges will there be in the basket in the end?
hints: Each turn, 4 apples come out and 3 oranges go in. So first count how many turns it takes to remove all 56 apples.
Number of turns = 56 ÷ 4. Each turn puts 3 oranges in the basket, so multiply the number of turns by 3.
Example: a basket has 10 apples. Each turn, 2 apples are swapped for 1 orange. That takes 10 ÷ 2 = 5 turns, so there are 5 × 1 = 5 oranges at the end.

stepByStep.text: Amey removes 4 apples each turn, so emptying 56 apples takes 56 ÷ 4 = 14 turns.
Each turn he puts in 3 oranges: 14 × 3 = 42.
So there will be 42 oranges in the basket in the end.

misconceptions.A: This is the correct answer. 14 rounds × 3 oranges = 42.

questionText: When a number P is divided by 6, the remainder is 2. When another number Q is divided by 6, the remainder is 5. What will the remainder be if P + Q is divided by 6?
hints: A remainder is what is left over after making groups of 6. When you add P and Q, their leftovers get added too.
P leaves 2 over and Q leaves 5 over, so together the leftovers are 2 + 5 = 7. But 7 is big enough to make another group of 6. What is left after that?
Example with dividing by 5: 8 leaves remainder 3 and 9 leaves remainder 4. The leftovers add to 3 + 4 = 7, which is one more group of 5 with 2 left. Check: 8 + 9 = 17, and 17 − 15 = 2.

stepByStep.text: P is some groups of 6 with 2 left over. Q is some groups of 6 with 5 left over.
Add them: P + Q is some groups of 6, with 2 + 5 = 7 left over.
7 makes one more group of 6, with 7 − 6 = 1 left over. Check with P = 8 and Q = 11: 8 + 11 = 19, and 19 − 18 = 1.
So the remainder when P + Q is divided by 6 is 1.

misconceptions.A: 0 would mean P+Q is divisible by 6, but 2+5=7, not 6.
misconceptions.B: This is the correct answer. Remainders add: 2+5=7, and 7 mod 6=1.
misconceptions.D: It CAN be found using remainder arithmetic.
